sources.title: The Code of Hammurabi (selected laws)
sources.author: Hammurabi, king of Babylon
sources.citation: Translated by L. W. King, The Code of Hammurabi (1915). Project Gutenberg eBook 17150.
sources.context: A block of diorite about 2.25 m tall, carved with 282 case rulings and set up in a temple. The laws below are a selection.
questions: Who is expected to enforce these rulings, and who is not?
What do laws 8, 196, and 200 suggest about how a person's rank affected the penalty?
Which of these laws rest on an appeal to a god or to ordeal rather than to witnesses?

sources.title: Babylon described
sources.author: Herodotus of Halicarnassus
sources.date: c. 430 BCE, describing an earlier city
sources.citation: The History of Herodotus, translated by G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book I.178–182. Project Gutenberg eBook 2707.
sources.context: Herodotus wrote about a city that had already been captured by the Persians. He probably never visited Babylon and relied on informants.
questions: Which measurements could in principle be checked against the ruins, and which could not?
Where does Herodotus signal that he doubts his own informants?
What might explain the size he reports for the walls?

sources.title: The tower in Shinar
sources.author: Hebrew tradition (anonymous)
sources.citation: Genesis 11:1–9, King James Version (1611). Public domain.
sources.context: A later tradition from outside Mesopotamia explains why a city there was left unfinished and why people speak different languages.
questions: How does this account treat the building of a city differently from the Babylonian laws?
What does it assume about a single city and the rest of the earth?
In what ways does this story agree with, and differ from, the Greek and Babylonian sources?
